title: Short Stuff: Blue Highway Signs
summary: Short Stuff episode on the blue highway logo signs in the United States. Josh and Chuck explain how the signs work: a three-part sequence (mainline sign listing available services, ramp sign at the exit, and trailblazer sign after the turn), the standardized size, and the fees companies pay that fund state programs (Tennessee and Virginia figures, Iowa's state-run program with rates unchanged since 1996, New Hampshire's large price hike, Nebraska and New Jersey per-sign costs). They cover eligibility rules (no movie theaters or adult businesses, tourist attractions allowed, distance limits, restroom, water and business-hours requirements, Florida's three- and six-mile priority rule) and the origin of the signs as a compromise under the Highway Beautification Act of 1965 backed by Lady Bird Johnson. They close with a comparison to junky homemade roadside signs and a trivia item on the order the signs appear. The episode includes some off-topic banter about Rush and Tom Cochran.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh opens the Short Stuff episode with a song joke and a brief reference to a 'Life is a Highway' singer.

segments.title: What blue highway signs are
segments.summary: Chuck describes the blue exit signs that list gas, food, lodging and specific brands like Burger King, Waffle House, BP and Motel 6. Josh notes the signs are standardized in size, about nineteen feet wide and ten feet tall.

segments.title: Off-topic banter about Canadian singer and Rush
segments.summary: The hosts joke about Tom Cochrane and Canada, then talk about the band Rush and a documentary about them.

segments.title: Signs as advertising and state funding
segments.summary: Chuck explains the signs are a form of advertising paid for by businesses. Josh gives state revenue figures, Tennessee about eight million dollars a year and Virginia six million, and says states earmark the money for the program. Iowa runs its program itself and has not raised rates since 1996, while about twenty states use contractors who take a cut of the gross.

segments.title: New Hampshire price hike and the three-sign sequence
segments.summary: The hosts discuss New Hampshire's sharp price increase under a contractor. They then explain the three parts of the sign system: the mainline sign showing available services, the ramp sign at the exit with brand logos, and the trailblazer sign after the turn. They settle that the ramp sign shows directions and the trailblazer is a separate sign after turning.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Brief transition into the ad break.

segments.title: Eligibility rules and spacing
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck explain that movie theaters and adult entertainment businesses are excluded, while tourist attractions such as wineries, museums and zoos can be included. Signs must be about 800 feet apart and cannot be near green distance signs or exit signs, which take priority.

segments.title: Distance and operating requirements
segments.summary: Florida gives priority to businesses within three miles of the exit and excludes those beyond six miles. Typical requirements include public restrooms, drinking water and regular business hours, with twenty-four-hour or seven-day businesses prioritized.

segments.title: Costs and the Highway Beautification Act
segments.summary: Costs vary by state: Nebraska about twelve hundred dollars per sign, New Jersey about twice that. The signs were a compromise under the Highway Beautification Act of October 1965, which Lyndon Johnson signed at the urging of his wife Lady Bird, after billboard limits were proposed and businesses objected.

segments.title: Billboards, roadside homemade signs, and graphic redesign
segments.summary: Chuck notes some states banned billboards, including Vermont, Hawaii and Alaska, and describes cluttered homemade roadside signs in rural Georgia. Josh mentions a New York graphic designer who redesigns those signs.

segments.title: Trivia on sign order and Roman Mars
segments.summary: Josh shares a trivia item from 99% Invisible that the blue signs always appear in the order camping, lodging, food, then gas. Chuck mentions Roman Mars.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up the Short Stuff episode.

segments.title: Credits
segments.summary: Chuck reads the show credits and iHeartRadio promotion.
